intro: Montmartre was an independent village, with its own town hall and vineyards, until Paris annexed it in 1860 to make it the 18th arrondissement. On this hill, the highest point in the city, painters with barely any money later moved in, along with a cabaret with a rabbit for an emblem and the only vineyard still growing inside Paris, while a white basilica slowly rose on the summit. It's about 2.5 km, with some slopes and stretches of stairs: Montmartre is, literally, a hill.
puntoPartida: Parvis of the Basilica of the Sacré-Cœur, at the top of the monumental staircase

paradas.titulo: The two riders guarding the entrance
paradas.llegada: Standing on the parvis, the large esplanade in front of the main façade of the Basilica of the Sacré-Cœur, with the monumental staircase behind you. Look up at the entrance portico, right above the doors.
paradas.enigma: This basilica is younger than it looks: construction began in 1875 and it wasn't consecrated until 1919, making it almost as recent as the Eiffel Tower. It was built with a special limestone brought from Château-Landon that secretes its own calcite every time it rains and effectively cleans itself, which is why it's still this white more than a century later, with barely any restoration. Now look at the portico of the main entrance: above it stand two bronze statues, each mounted on horseback. How many equestrian statues flank the entrance?
pistas: They're up high, one on each side of the entrance portico, above the doors.
You can count them on one hand and have fingers left over.
There are 2 equestrian statues: Joan of Arc and Saint Louis.
paradas.historia: The two statues were added in 1927, the work of sculptor Hippolyte Lefebvre: Joan of Arc, sword raised, and King Saint Louis IX, gesturing toward justice. The whole basilica was built as a kind of collective vow after France's defeat by Prussia in 1870 and the Paris Commune uprising of 1871: a way of starting over, quite literally, from the highest point in the city.
paradas.fuente: Basilique du Sacré-Cœur de Montmartre; Wikipédia

paradas.titulo: The town hall of a village that no longer exists
paradas.llegada: Walk around behind the basilica for a couple of minutes to Place du Tertre, the painters' square, with its awnings and dozens of easels.
paradas.enigma: Before 1860, Montmartre wasn't a Paris neighbourhood: it was a village with its own town hall, market gardens and windmills, surrounded by open countryside. This very square, now taken over by portrait painters and café terraces, was its administrative centre. Look on one of the façades around the square for the plaque marking where Montmartre's first town hall once stood. What year does the plaque give for when it was set up there?
pistas: It's a year from the late 18th century, long before Montmartre became part of Paris.
It starts with 179.
The plaque says 1790.
paradas.historia: The village of Montmartre kept its own mayor, its own church and even its own vineyards until 1 January 1860, when it was annexed to Paris along with the surrounding towns to create today's twenty arrondissements. Decades later, that independent spirit survived in its own way: local artists founded the tongue-in-cheek "Commune Libre de Montmartre", which still holds public festivals today and appoints its own honorary mayor.
paradas.fuente: Mairie du 18e arrondissement de Paris; Ville de Paris

paradas.llegada: Walk west from Place du Tertre, along rue Norvins and then rue Ravignan, to Place Émile-Goudeau, a small stepped square with a circular bench wrapped around a lamppost.
paradas.enigma: This is where the Bateau-Lavoir once stood, a ramshackle wooden building where Montmartre's poorest artists lived and worked in the early 20th century: Picasso painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon here in 1907, the picture that opened the door to Cubism. It got its name, "laundry boat", because its irregular maze of corridors and windows, seen from a certain angle, resembled the laundry barges that once floated on the Seine, where Paris washerwomen did their washing. The original wooden building burned to the ground in 1970. Look at the one in front of you, rebuilt after that fire: what is it made of instead, unlike the original?
pistas: The original was wood, which burns easily. This one no longer is.
It's the same grey material most modern buildings are made from.
The current building is made of concrete.
paradas.historia: The 1970 fire gutted the Bateau-Lavoir a year after it had been listed as a historic monument. The rebuild, finished in 1978, reproduced the original façade and layout, but in concrete, precisely so it could never burn the same way again. Today it's still used for exactly what it always was, artists' studios, though none quite as poor or as unknown as Picasso or Modigliani were here.

paradas.titulo: The windmill that climbed onto a roof
paradas.llegada: From Place Émile-Goudeau, head up toward rue Lepic (via rue Ravignan or rue d'Orchampt) and keep climbing to the corner with rue Girardon. Look for windmill sails: impossible to miss.
paradas.enigma: Montmartre once had around 30 windmills, most for grinding grain, a few for pressing grapes. Today only two survive, and this is one of them: the Moulin Radet. But look closely at exactly where it's sitting, because it isn't where you'd expect to find a real windmill. Where is the mill actually standing, instead of resting on the ground like any other?
respuestas: on the roof of a building
pistas: Look for its foundations: you won't find them at street level.
It's several metres above your head, not at your height.
The mill sits on top of a building's roof, not on the ground.
paradas.historia: This mill and its neighbour, the Blute-fin, a little further on behind a wall, belonged from 1809 to the Debray family, who in the 19th century turned them into a guinguette, a popular open-air dance hall with wine, named Moulin de la Galette. Renoir painted it in 1876; Van Gogh and Toulouse-Lautrec painted it too: a mill that stopped grinding grain to grind out, for decades, entire Sundays of dancing instead.
paradas.fuente: Mairie du 18e arrondissement; Wikipédia — Moulin de la Galette

paradas.titulo: The rabbit that escaped the pot
paradas.llegada: Continue along rue Girardon to rue Saint-Vincent and follow it to the corner with rue des Saules. Look for a small pink-fronted house with green shutters.
paradas.enigma: This is Au Lapin Agile, a cabaret that's been welcoming artists, poets and singers since the 19th century: Picasso, Modigliani and Utrillo all crossed paths within these same walls. Above the door hangs a sign painted in 1875 by caricaturist André Gill: a rabbit in a green coat and cap, leaping out of a cooking pot with a bottle in its paw. Look closely at the rabbit's neck, where it wears a knotted scarf. What colour is it?
pistas: It isn't green, like its coat, or black, like the pot.
It's the same colour as the red wine in its paw.
The rabbit's scarf is red.
paradas.historia: Gill's sign gave the place its name: people started calling it "le lapin à Gill" (Gill's rabbit), which over time turned into "Lapin Agile" (agile rabbit). The owner, Frédéric Gérard, known as Père Frédé, let anyone with a song or a poem take the stage; tradition has it that Picasso settled the odd unpaid bill with paintings, including one titled, fittingly, Au Lapin Agile.

paradas.titulo: The vineyard that saved an artists' neighbourhood
paradas.llegada: Cross rue des Saules: right opposite, behind a fence, rows of vines climb the slope. This is the Clos Montmartre, the city's vineyard.
paradas.enigma: Inside the Paris city limits, there's practically no vineyard left, except this one: a patch of under a quarter hectare with more than a thousand gamay and pinot noir vines. It isn't a medieval leftover that happened to survive. When this plot was about to become an apartment block, local artists and residents, organised as the Commune Libre du Vieux Montmartre, got the city to replant a vineyard here from scratch. Look for the sign or plaque at the entrance to the Clos: what year was this vineyard planted?
pistas: It's a year from the 1930s, not the Middle Ages.
It's just a couple of years before 1935.
The current vineyard was planted in 1933.
paradas.historia: The first grape harvest festival was held in 1934, with the President of the Republic, Albert Lebrun, among the crowd. Montmartre's harvest festival is still held every October, with parades and several thousand visitors, though the wine it produces, barely a few hundred bottles a year, is almost always sold at charity auctions: here the grapes matter less than the symbol that a vineyard can still grow in the middle of Paris.
paradas.fuente: Mairie du 18e arrondissement — Le Clos Montmartre; Ville de Paris

paradas.titulo: The sea gods at the foot of the basilica
paradas.llegada: Head back toward the basilica along rue Saint-Vincent and rue du Chevalier-de-la-Barre, then go down the steps of Square Louise-Michel, the terraced garden that runs down the hill's south slope beside the funicular. Look for the large stone fountain on the upper terrace.
paradas.enigma: This monumental fountain, finished in 1932, is dedicated to the gods of the sea. Below the terrace where you're standing, several grotto-shaped niches open up in the stone, side by side; in each one, a sea creature, half man and half fish, holds up a basin that water spills from into the large pool below. Count the niches with sea creatures in them. How many are there?
pistas: They sit side by side, forming a row beneath the upper terrace.
It's a small number, the same as the number of sides on a triangle.
There are 3 niches with sea creatures.
paradas.historia: Sculptor Paul Gasq signed this neoclassical fountain, dedicated to Tritons and naiads holding up water above grottoes carved straight into the wall's stone. The garden it stands in changed its name in 2004: it used to be called Square Willette, after a local painter, but the city renamed it Square Louise-Michel, honouring the anarchist who fought in the 1871 Paris Commune, the same Commune that, indirectly, led to the white basilica now crowning the staircase above your head.
paradas.fuente: Ville de Paris — Square Louise-Michel; Wikipédia — Fontaine Paul Gasq

paradas.titulo: The five domes that close the circle
paradas.llegada: Climb back up the staircase (or take the funicular) to the basilica's parvis, the same spot where the route began. Step back a little from the portico, toward the edge of the esplanade, until you can see the whole cluster of domes above the roofline.
paradas.enigma: You're back where you started, but look up with different eyes this time. Architect Paul Abadie designed the basilica in the shape of a Greek cross, crowned by a much larger central dome representing Christ, surrounded by smaller ones representing the four evangelists. Count every dome you can see from here, the large one and the small ones together. How many are there in total?
pistas: Add the large central dome to the smaller ones around it.
It's an odd number, between 4 and 6.
There are 5 domes in total: 1 large and 4 small.
paradas.historia: In the bell tower, off to one side, hangs La Savoyarde, a 19-tonne bell cast in Annecy in 1895 and donated by the four dioceses of Savoy, one of the heaviest in France. There's a curious coincidence behind that gift: Savoy was annexed to France in 1860, the very same year that Montmartre, the independent village you've just walked through, was annexed to Paris. Two annexations, the same year, unknowingly tied together by a bell and by this white hill.
paradas.fuente: Basilique du Sacré-Cœur de Montmartre; Wikipédia

final.titulo: You've climbed to Paris's last village
final.texto: From a portico with two bronze riders to a vineyard under a quarter hectare that refused to disappear, by way of a building that's no longer made of wood and a rabbit with a red scarf round its neck. Montmartre stopped being a village in 1860, but for a century and a half it's managed to keep looking like one anyway. The white hill now above your head has watched windmills, penniless painters and an entire city grow up around it, never quite managing to swallow it whole.
